title: AI powered entomology: Lessons from millions of AI code reviews — Tomas Reimers, Graphite
talk_summary: Graphite built an AI code reviewer and found that raw LLM review comments are noisy because models produce both useful defects and pedantic best-practice suggestions. They narrowed prompts to comment classes that LLMs can catch and humans actually want, then measured quality via downvotes and whether comments led to code changes.

takeaways.what_they_do: Classify review comments by whether the LLM can catch them and whether humans want to receive them, then prompt only for the top-right quadrant: real bugs, accidental committed code, performance/security, and code-doc mismatches.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we updated our prompts to only prompt the LLM to do things that were in its capacity and that humans wanted to receive.

takeaways.what_they_do: Measure the percent of review comments that lead to the code change they describe within the PR, and compare the bot against a human baseline.
takeaways.numbers: Human comments ~50% led to changes; bot reached 52% as of March

takeaways.what_they_do: Let developers react to AI review comments; downvote spikes indicate hallucination or overreach, prompting prompt/model tuning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: When we start to see a downvote spike, we know that okay, we might be trying to extend this thing beyond its capabilities.

takeaways.what_they_do: Continuously check whether new models or larger context keep review comments in the desired capability/desirability quadrant.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as we got into Claude 4 or Opus instead of Sonnet, how do we know that we're actually staying in this top right quadrant?

takeaways.what_they_do: Explicitly exclude comments that are always technically correct but unwelcome from bots, such as add tests, extract logic, or add comments.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You should add a comment describing what this class does. You should extract this logic out into a function or you should make sure this code has tests.
